newsitem.title: DUBAI: UAE issues tender for lucrative deal to boost navy.
newsitem.headline: UAE issues tender for lucrative deal to boost navy.

text.p: The United Arab Emirates, a key arms buyer, has issued a tender for frigates, ships and fast patrol boats in a deal worth up to $2 billion, industry executives said on Wednesday.
"They have put out a tender for a deal that will probably be worth between $1.5 billion and $2 billion," one said.
The package includes six frigates, 100 fast patrol boats and several minesweepers, the executives said.
UAE officials were not available to comment.

International firms including the United States's Newport News Shipbuilding, a subsidiary of Tenneco Inc and Dutch state-owned shipyard Koninklijke Schelde Groep are competing for the contract, the executives said.
Manufacturers of radar devices, communications equipment, weapons systems and propulsion units that will complement the vessels also stand to profit from the deal, they said.
The UAE is one of the world's most lucrative arms markets. It spent about $6 billion in the 1987-94 period on arms imports and more deals are in the pipeline.
The executives and diplomats said the tender is part of the UAE's efforts to bolster naval defences against a potential threat from Iran, a powerful neighbour across the Gulf.
Abu Dhabi and Tehran are locked in a dispute over three strategic Gulf islands located near key oil shipping lanes. Iran has angered the UAE by building up its presence on the islands.

"Diplomatic efforts with Iran have failed so the UAE is building up its navy as a deterrent against Iran," said an executive in the UAE capital Abu Dhabi. "The fast-attack patrol boats could...work as a deterrent to Iran's plans to buy submarines."
Iran is to receive its third Russian-made Kilo-class submarine at the end of 1996 which will enhance its ability to control Gulf waterways.
"The UAE has a long coast that is not very secure," said another executive when asked about the effectiveness of the fast patrol boats.
But another executive said the UAE also had other concerns.

"The patrol boats would be very effective in attacking large ships. They have a low profile and they move quickly," he said. "Iran is a concern but there are other issues such as the infiltration of illegal immigrants, drugs and smuggling."
Nearly 150,000 illegal workers have left the UAE ahead of a new law cracking down on unlawful foreign labour.
